text:
The three days of travel are presented as a kind of suspended sentence. Outwardly nothing happens, and yet everything of significance happens. Emphasis falls upon the servants, the wood, the knife, and the fire; and by that emphasis the instruments of the act are named before the act itself occurs. Obedience and horror are kept together in the story from first to last, and neither is ever suffered to prevail over the other. Faith in this story is a structured relation; it is no feeling.

Compared with the earlier promise, the scene shows less difference than first appears. The reader is reminded that Isaac is the child of the covenant, the one through whom the nations are to be blessed; and the promise is then turned into a test. The whole scene turns upon a single word, _hineni_, "here I am," which Abraham speaks three times: once to God, once to Isaac, once to the angel. Each time the word means something different, and each time it costs him more. In this story the language of being present is also the language of loss.
